speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: After he retired, he continues to volunteer to pass down his wisdom.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Today, he is a cornerstone of Kebun Baru’s Yellow Ribbon outreach.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Alice, aged 70, spent her entire life as a nurse.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: From 1986 to 2000, she built the modern ambulance service that we know.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Today, she still leads our community emergency responders.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: All of us here within this Chamber have met incredible seniors, their stories etched in our minds.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Some have done great things; some have lead simple but meaningful lives.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Our Pioneers, soon to be followed by our Baby Boomers, are now growing old.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They have been described as the coming Silver Tsunami.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: An ageing population presents major challenges to an unprepared society: less economic vitality, higher tax burden on the young, and an intergenerational fight for resources between the young and old.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But we, at PAP.SG, believe that we must and we will meet these serious challenges and then go beyond.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Besides the challenges, we should also focus on the positives.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: More and more of our seniors are highly-skilled and experienced, with a stronger ability to retire productively and to contribute to society.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And this is what we believe to be the Silver Dividend.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But creating this Silver Dividend requires a lot of work.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We need to stretch our minds, stretch our hearts and stretch our hands.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: If we are successful, our seniors can shine brightly in their autumn years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They can reflect on their lifelong experiences, in comfort and dignity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They can pass down their very special spark to the next generation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And that is how we can build a wise and resilient Singapore ‒ through values and experiences passed down by each generation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: On what basis does PAP.SG have this confidence?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Well, Singapore is not the first or the only society dealing with the challenge of ageing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Successful preparations require decisive actions and long-term planning.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Before this Silver Tsunami has hit Singapore, we have assembled the major policy pieces.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In percentages, I believe we have undergone the most aggressive healthcare expansion in recent memory in any developed country.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Three, we have strengthened MediShield Life and are reviewing ElderShield Life.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Four, we have improved retirement adequacy through higher Central Provident Fund (CPF) payouts.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Five, we have introduced lease buy-back for seniors living in many Housing and Development Board (HDB) flats through the enhanced Silver Housing Bonus.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But as we frequently say in this Chamber, we are not done building Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Much has been done, but there is much more to do.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It is in this spirit that my fellow PAP.SG Members and I would like to put forward additional ideas for consideration.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Today, we will talk about retirement adequacy, retirement housing, seniors’ employability, volunteerism, the digital divide, digital medicine and caregiver support.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We are fully aware that meeting the challenge of ageing is expensive.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, some of us worry deeply about how to pay for meeting our promises to our seniors while still creating a bright future for our children.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, whatever we do today or put in place tomorrow must be prudent and sustainable.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Otherwise, we will be loading an unfair burden on future generations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Fortunately, the key to success requires more than Government dollars.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It requires society to come together to create community initiatives to support our seniors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As such, my fellow PAP.SG Members and I will speak about our community initiatives for seniors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We believe in these initiatives and we want them to spread across Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Even now, many of us are seeing our parents age.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: When I speak to my peers, a common theme emerges.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Dad once carried us on his shoulders, but he is looking so frail recently.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Mum used to nag us not to forget this or that, but now she is also forgetting things.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And we start wondering what we would do when they can no longer take care of themselves.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We would all like to take care of them at home.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But sometimes it is not possible for medical, financial or family reasons.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: A friend told me that he looked into some nursing homes, but the seniors there looked so sad that he could not bear to.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They were given basic care but could not pursue their own interests or social life.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Nobody cared about what they wanted or what makes them unique and what gets them out of bed every day.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In other words, they are okay but they have lost their dignity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This is not the only way seniors have lost their dignity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Seniors lose their dignity when they cannot pay for their retirement years; when they have to move to somewhere more affordable and leave their social circles.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Seniors lose dignity when they are viewed as burdens to society.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Many seniors feel that if they lose dignity, a longer life is not a blessing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Mother Teresa said, "Being unwanted, unloved, uncared for, forgotten by everybody, I think that is a much greater hunger, a much greater poverty than the person who has nothing to eat." I am sure none of us want our parents and our nation's Pioneers to be in this state, and we certainly do not want to be in this state one day.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: With that in mind, I would like to propose three policy changes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: My first proposal is to strengthen affordable, dignified living options for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Some nursing homes that are built long ago still have many seniors sharing a room.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At some homes, overworked staff do not have time to say "Hi" or chat.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The lack of autonomy, meaning and privacy in many nursing and retirement homes is a huge factor why eight in 10 Singaporeans worry about getting old, and why many of us still view these homes as "dumping" our parents there.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But when Singaporeans genuinely cannot take care of their parents at home, they should not have to feel that they are unfilial.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Fortunately, we are beginning to see new types of nursing homes and seniors housing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, with regard to nursing homes, I believe that we are making an important transition and there had been some solid success.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, we have created the new Kampung Admiralty for HDB dwellers who want a comfortable assisted living home option.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Kampung Admiralty has senior housing built on top of a common community plaza with a hawker centre and medical facilities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The designers also wisely put the senior activity centre next to the kindergarten.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I visited Kampung Admiralty with some of my architect friends to study the layout.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that we can build many more Kampung Admiraltys.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They can serve as our mothership to surrounding blocks of conventional flats and be the anchor to our Kampung for All Ages.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I am also glad to hear that Minister Gan Kim Yong is looking into various assisted living options for more Singaporeans, just like the options offered at Kampung Admiralty.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Today, we also have many more choices in nursing homes, which I consider a partial success.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We must make more of such options more affordable.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We also had experiments on private retirement homes or assisted living arrangements, although I feel that we have not yet discovered the right model.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I have been following a site at Jurong Kechil that has been billed as a potential retirement home.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But because the developer had to bid against conventional residential developments, some have questioned whether it will turn out to be more a condominium than a retirement home.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We need to quickly assemble a full range of good options, at different price points, for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Both our seniors living in HDB and private estates must have choices to either age-in-place, right-size to a right place, live in an assisted living environment or a retirement village, or move into a nursing home.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: A senior lecturer in the National University of Singapore (NUS), who was part of the group advising me on senior housing, shared this with me, "Please tell the Government that this is urgent.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We are getting older and older every day.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There is no time for us to wait for more reviews and more studies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We need these choices now." After studying the existing gaps and options, I would like to propose four ways for the Government to create a broader range of choices.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We can design it so that only properly regulated players can bid.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: These players, as an industry, must offer various price points.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: How do we make sure that there is no race to the bottom?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The Government can charge property tax based on the revenue intensity of their operations, which depends on the price point of their offering.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But today we already ascribe different values to industrial parks, schools and public housing because they are important to our society.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We can experiment with a few projects and then finetune along the way.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There are also ways to further ringfence the cost to the rest of the society through creative land use, such as allowing for usage in certain religious lands – I know a particular church that is very keen to explore doing so.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We can also look at spaces on top of car parks, spaces between HDB blocks.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Two, the Government can put in watertight regulations on what constitutes a retirement home, even without a separate land use category.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The Government must get developers to clearly spell out what assisted services, service standards and pricing to offer.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But it will be a partial solution because the existing land use category is unlikely to rule out non-seniors from buying.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And there is always the temptation from speculators or shoebox apartment buyers to price genuine senior buyers out.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Specifically, we can look at the Retirement Village Acts in both Queensland and Victoria states.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Pearl Bank is a condominium with a deep sense of community and unique architecture value.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It is also very near Singapore General Hospital.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There has been talk about En bloc and conservation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, they are constrained from doing so, at least through the En bloc route, because they have maximised their GFA under the current regulations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: If the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) can view them as potential retirement residential development, can these regulations be relaxed?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond Pearl Bank, I am sure there are other private estates that could voluntarily work with the Government to be converted into a full or partial retirement residential development.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: My second proposal is to help our seniors, especially those living in private estates, monetise their housing assets.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Seniors lose dignity when they cannot afford to pay for their retirement years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For many Singaporeans, our most major asset is our home.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Monetisation options are in place for seniors living in 4-room HDB or smaller flats but not for seniors in other housing types.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In my constituency, there is a private estate called Teachers’ Estate.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As the name tells you, the seniors there are mostly retired teachers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But now, some of them are asset-rich and cash-poor.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They do not qualify for most assistance schemes because they live in private estates.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They tell me that they do have the option of downsizing but it is hard to find affordable options nearby which can also free up enough money for retirement.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: When they move, they are cut off from their social circles.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, we need to look into more options that enable them to age-in-place.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Again, why has the market not provided such an option?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For many retirees living in private housing, they live frugally, so they might only need tens of thousands of dollars each year in retirement.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Talking to the private and people sector, I see at least two solutions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The first is to get the Government to encourage and regulate social enterprises or co-operatives (co-ops) to undertake such reverse mortgages.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The social enterprises and co-ops can also securitise their assets in the financial markets, and this can be done, given Singapore’s status as a centre for real estate investment trusts (REITS).

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Government regulations can also ensure that the social enterprises or co-ops are properly capitalised, the reverse mortgage valuation process is proper, the fees are transparent and appropriate, and we can also push the social enterprises or co-ops to go for transparency and accountability, perhaps by getting them to declare a socially acceptable and transparent cost-plus financing model.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The second solution is for the Government to encourage and regularise specialised funds for seniors to monetise their assets.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We can look at the innovation happening in France.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Retirees sell their assets to a fund that is based on the French concept of "Viager" property contracts.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Seniors sell their asset to a fund which owns a portfolio of properties.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: While the property deed goes to the fund, the seniors have the right to stay in the property until they pass on one day.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Based on market valuation, actuarial studies and the fund’s desired returns, the fund pays the senior an upfront payment, followed by a lifelong annuity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We can even consider adding life insurance payoffs into the housing equity to increase the amount of assets that seniors can monetise.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The Government can also consider regulating how the funds are capitalised, to make sure that the funds are not over-leveraged, the transparency of the returns and the actuarial basis of the fund payoff.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: My third proposal is to introduce senior caregiver leave.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Seniors lose dignity when their loved ones are not with them in times of need.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Ageing, falling sick and one day departing from the world are a fate we all share.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This would come with costs to the companies but there are ways to limit the costs to deserving situations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: One, we can limit it to Singaporeans with parents aged above 70.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Two, we can limit it to eligible Singaporeans who have less than 14 days of annual leave, because these Singaporeans have even less time to care for their parents compared to others.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Three, at the start, focus on companies with more than 100 employees.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Four, adopt a tripartite process to deliberate on this.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As mentioned earlier, Government programmes are only part of the equation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There is much opportunity to share best practices.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It brings the do-gooders of Kebun Baru together, whether they are Government agencies, voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs), grassroots committees or even new groups of volunteers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, they have brought their strengths together and brought seniors to our Community Centre for regular meals.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The seniors loved the food and the meals broke their social isolation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Now, Project Starfish and Mummy Yummy are bringing in more student volunteers through Hope Collective so that they can expand their outreach.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They are also working with the Police to share the workload.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Through the Hope Collective, we can also take a comprehensive view and plug in the gaps.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Overall, our vision is to build a culture of respect, love and care for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We want to build "a Kampung for All Ages".

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I am looking forward to learning more ideas from my colleagues in this session.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Some medical professionals say our elder care has to catch up with First World standards.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I say we should and then go beyond that.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Just as our seniors have built a world-beating economy for us, we can be the world leader in building a senior-friendly society for them.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It seems like a tall order, until we remember that everybody has parents and everybody will grow old.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, everybody has a vested interest in getting this sorted out.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: If the Government can provide the right structure, it will unleash the society’s energy to do so.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, the three ideas I have laid out today will do precisely that.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Of course, ageing presents serious challenges, even for a nation as united and organised as Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But we should not shy away from meeting these challenges.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As Prime Minister Lee said in his 2014 National Day Rally speech, "At the heart of the Singapore Story is our belief in Singapore; a belief that we can turn vulnerability and despair into confidence and hope; belief that out of the trauma of Separation, we can build a modern metropolis and a beautiful home." What I would like to ask this Chamber today is, "What is a beautiful home?" It is a place where we can live with dignity, no matter our age; where we can rest assured that we can take care of our families; where the community does right by those who sacrificed their best years for us.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Because only when we have done that, can we say this is home, truly.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It is about a change of policies and communities willing to assist seniors live meaningfully and independently and be assets to society and country throughout their silver years.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The strategy is a call for affirmative concepts of people of all ages, a society for all ages that celebrates and prepares properly for the whole population so that everyone can be healthy, active, positive and productive individuals throughout life.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Every citizen can contribute to the public good, helping themselves and others, as well as striving for positive fulfilment through meaningful engagement.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In our population demography, there are many positive opportunities that we can tap on, from the large numbers of healthy and active seniors in our society, to be workers, mentors, caregivers, child minders, consumers and volunteers.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: To successfully manage the economics of our ageing population, we need good forward planning and strategic policy choices that have the cooperation from all sectors of our society.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: People are capable of living self-reliant lives with new possibilities that make living exciting and productive through the right policies in labour market participation, social inclusion as well as healthcare in place.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: We need policies that can enable and support all ages to enjoy physical, social and mental well-being.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: As a start, we need to change the prevalent negative discriminatory attitudes towards our seniors as useless, as a ticking demographic time bomb and as a burden that society can ill-afford.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Senior citizens should be viewed as assets who can be tapped on for their wisdom, experience, values and expertise.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: There is evidence that longer working lives have beneficial effects on an individual’s physical and psychological well-being.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Some evidence also show that a worker’s productivity does not necessarily decline with age; any decline in physical capacity is often compensated by qualities and skills acquired through experience.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In essence, it is health status rather than age that is a key factor in determining productivity levels.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This will make the country the worst hit of a dozen economies in the report even though it was Japan that has recorded the biggest workforce decline over the past 10 years.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Given our shrinking workforce, it will be good if we can increase the labour participation of seniors.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Active labour market participation may be enhanced by establishing flexible retirement arrangements: through forming a working environment that is suitable to the needs of all generations, continuous education, promoting positive images of senior employees and anti-discrimination policies, and recognising and lowering barriers of entry into the workforce so as to include the seniors in our economy.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In this report, it says that many seniors want to work beyond the official retirement age to remain financially independent and to keep themselves active.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Seniors hope to have meaningful job opportunities to fulfil their aspirations at their stage of life.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: These are all good recommendations and I hope that our Government can consider them and make them available soonest.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: There are health and social benefits in volunteering.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It offers seniors significant physical, emotional and cognitive or brain health benefits.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It also enhances social support and social inclusion.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The brain is involved in feeling as well as thinking, and this means that finding meaningful and purposeful activity is particularly important.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This can be accomplished through volunteering by finding roles that are personally meaningful.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Matching and placing volunteers in the best role for each individual is worth the effort.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Many studies have found that engaging in voluntary work in later life is a strong predictor of better self-rated health, daily functioning, physical activity and life satisfaction.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Voluntary work in later life is also associated with a decrease in depression, hypertension and mortality among seniors.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In addition to health benefits, volunteering can enhance social support networks, increase social status and reinforce knowledge and skills.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Volunteering also provides a role identity and sense of purpose for those retired from paid work.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Seniors can better integrate socially when they find structures for volunteering.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: There is a need to increase awareness of opportunities and community needs and to facilitate opportunities for engagement.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: People are looking for a range of options where they can see the value and impact of their contributions in their community.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: More people are interested in group volunteering, short-term assignments, as well as virtual volunteering, and they view volunteering as a way of transferring or gaining skills.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Some of our SkillsFuture Credit courses can be tailored for this purpose.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Let us promote and provide avenues for volunteering as a meaningful occupation that provides direction as well as purpose and passion, just like the fulfilment that comes from meaningful paid work where individuals find fulfilment, meaning and personal identity.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This form of volunteering can be viewed as "serious leisure", "career volunteering" or "career redirection".

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: (f) Environmental volunteering may be ideal for adults who are interested in environmental issues, collecting information about the environment.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The National Environment Agency (NEA), Town Councils and Community Centres may recruit such volunteers and even for just one-day events.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: (g) Employer-supported volunteering, where corporations support the commitment of their employees for activities through “community day or days” each year.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: These can be further encouraged in quality and quantity and in having more businesses, especially small and medium enterprises (SMEs) involved.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: (h) Retired Employee volunteering programme, where workplaces that have alumni or retiree programmes can incorporate volunteer opportunities.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Our Ministries can pilot such programmes where employees can continue as mentors, volunteering especially to ease the transition of new employees.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It will be useful to have a volunteer centre with coordinators to offer programmes that appeal to different groups with different interests and to match and place the volunteering services with the community groups and organisations.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This will provide a one-stop convenient avenue and will maximise outcome.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Senior adults may experience challenges and barriers to volunteering in relation to transportation, scheduling issues and out-of-pocket expenses.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Health is defined as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely by the absence of disease and infirmity.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Seniors considered the deterioration in their physical or mental health as the biggest threat to their well-being.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: As life expectancy increases, it becomes more important that the added years to life are accompanied by good health.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Good health is a prerequisite for anyone expecting an active and fulfilling life.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Chronic diseases, especially diabetes and hypertension, are considered one of the most significant health challenges in developed countries and represent a major component of service activity and expenditure, as well as a major contributor to disability, ill-health and mortality among the older population in these countries.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Many of these are also key risk factors for the development of dementia.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It has been reported that the cumulative lifetime disability for those who smoke, are obese and do not exercise is four times greater than those who are of a healthy weight, exercise and do not smoke.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Traditionally, models of care have tended to focus on those with the most medical needs.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I would like our Government to ensure subsequent future service provisions reverse this trend so that equal priority is accorded to both medical treatment and the promotion of health and well-being.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Shifting the focus towards promotion of lifelong good health would lead to a significant increase not only in life expectancy but also in disability-free life expectancy.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: So, the emphasis of our healthcare policy should be to prevent and reduce disability and premature mortality by supporting the development and implementation of policies towards this aim.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: While there is evidence that it is difficult to change the behaviour patterns of seniors, research has also found that changes in lifestyle, even in later years, can bring health benefits.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Research indicates that retirement tends to decrease the level of physical activity needed for a healthy lifestyle.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Social isolation may contribute to depression, grief, stress, anxiety, alcoholism and medication misuse, failure to seek help when needed, and an extremely high suicide rate, particularly among older men.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In its submission to the Second World Assembly on Ageing 2002, the World Health Organisation observed that age-friendly built environments for people with disabilities facilitate access to the appropriate range of housing and housing-related support services that are delivered in an integrated and sustainable manner.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This promotes equality of opportunity, individual choice and independent living.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: These can make a difference between independency and dependency for all individuals and is particularly important for those growing older.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: For instance, older people who live in an unsafe environment or areas with multiple physical barriers are less likely to venture out and are, therefore, more prone to isolation, depression, reduced fitness and increased mobility problems.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It will be good if HDB continues to promote and support universally recognised seniors-oriented housing designs and compositions that allow for an environment that may be easily accessed and used to the greatest possible extent by persons of any age or having any particular physical, sensory, medical ill-health or disability.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: We must try to design and develop seniors-friendly living spaces and buildings which are suitable for their physical and social needs.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Common spaces with consideration for a micro-community with, for example, recreation and community areas to enable seniors to lend support to one another and to engage with one another will prevent social isolation.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Support services within the same block or close vicinity that are useful are Seniors Activity Centres, clinics, minimarts and food outlets.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: There is an increasing recognition that new technologies can offer new ways of supporting people with medical illnesses and disabilities and facilitating them to continue living independently at home.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: They can play an important role in self-care and prevention of advancing disability.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Mobility is a key determinant towards an individual’s ability to access social or physical services and to engage in community activities.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Seniors who live in inaccessible environments are less likely to go outdoors and are, therefore, more prone to isolation, depression, reduced fitness and mobility problems.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, let us continue to enhance a seniors-friendly public transport system.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Let us continue to aim for a community that is inclusive of everyone, including especially our seniors.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Let our seniors be welcomed by society, businesses and community alike.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Let our seniors be respected, not patronised, and let the wealth of knowledge and experience they have to offer be valued.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope our Government will consider my suggestions above and implement measures towards achieving an even better society for all.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I join my colleagues in this hon House in support of the Motion and echo their proposition to recognise that seniors are a gift to us.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, seniors should be respected, even if they cannot contribute anymore.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The success, stability and economic benefits enjoyed by us today have been built upon the sacrifices, sweat and tears of our seniors.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: They suffered loss so that we might gain.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: As a country, we owe it to our seniors to enjoy their golden years in dignity.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: More fundamentally, as individuals, we owe it to our parents to enjoy their golden years in dignity.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Regrettably, it appears there are some among us who do not agree with that statement.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We have all seen many, too many, cases of neglect or abuse of seniors by their adult or even middle-aged children.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Yes, there might be bad blood between a senior and his or her children.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding that, few among us will condone neglect or abuse of such seniors by their adult children.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Accordingly, Mr Deputy Speaker, whilst I firmly believe that filial piety cannot be legislated, I submit that Singapore needs a more robust and coordinated framework towards ensuring that our seniors will be well taken care of.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Caring for a person is not about how lovable a person is, or how fragrant the person is, or how affordable or convenient it is to care for the person.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Particularly in the context of a parent and child, it is about love and obligation.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And obligation, even if there is no love.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: As a community, therefore, we must continue to emphasise the value of filial piety.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Parents should set the example, and it should be taught in schools and religious institutions.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We should also recognise that with or without filial piety, financial dependence on children can strain and has frequently strained parent-child relationships.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, let us empower seniors to take control of their financial assets in order to reduce financial dependence on their children.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Whilst it is understandable that seniors would like to give properties to their children, the gifts can be made after they have passed on.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We should intensify and expand our ground efforts to inform seniors of the advantages of the reverse mortgage to HDB and other financial institutions and encourage a higher greater take-up rate.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The payouts from the reverse mortgage will enable the seniors to reduce their dependence on public assistance or their children.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The remaining value of the flat can still be gifted to their children after they have passed on.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We should encourage seniors to maintain themselves out of their own properties.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: They should not make gifts to their children in their lifetime.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: By making a Will, the senior can continue to own and enjoy their property and leave the remainder, after they have passed on, to their children.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: By using the Will, the senior retains to a large extent the control over his or her assets and finances, and financial independence.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, some children may not be happy to wait so long.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If the parent-child relationship deteriorates because the parent had decided to take control of his or her own finances, then all the more the parent would have made the correct decision.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Generally speaking, parents will express their love for their children by bestowing things to them.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: As a result, many seniors transfer their properties to their children.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Only after they do so, do they come to realise that their children are not filial, and they are even mistreated, abused, neglected or even abandoned.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Even if it does not go to such an extreme extent, parent-child relationship often deteriorates as a result of financial or money issues.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In order to avoid conflicts, seniors should be urged to reduce their financial dependence on their children.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In their lifetime, they should not transfer or give away their financial assets to their children.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: They should be encouraged to make a will to allocate their inheritance.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Seniors can take up the reverse mortgage through HDB.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Not only will they avoid paying the instalments, but also, they will receive monthly payouts.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: They should make a will in order to allocate their remaining inheritance.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: There is another benefit of making a will.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The will can be amended at any time.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The filial children can receive more inheritance, whereas the unfilial children can be written out of the will.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If the children are unhappy with such arrangements, it proves even more that your decision is correct.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This is an important power, considering that family relations could be further aggravated where applications are made by parents against their children.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Where the Commissioner has sufficient evidence at hand, the Commissioner should make the application, notwithstanding that the parent may not be willing to adduce any evidence against their children.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: When an order for maintenance is made and not complied with, the Act provides a further mechanism in which securities can be made and ordered out of existing properties.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This is also extremely useful and assists the seniors without having to make another round or commence another round of legal proceedings.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Whilst we are not in any position to legislate filial piety, and we should not, as Prof Walter Woon pointed out in his speech during the Second Reading of the Maintenance of Parents Bill in 1994, we can provide a safety net if filial piety fails.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Here, I may add that, in my view, the Vulnerable Adults Bill in the form presented to this House at its First Reading is inadequate in that it fails to legislate financial protection for vulnerable adults, including the elderly.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I hope to hear more from the Minister on this issue.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: At this point, allow me to share a couple of stories which I constructed from incidents made known to me.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: He and his wife had three children, whom they provided for and raised.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Before Mr Tan passed away, he added the name of his eldest son as a joint owner of the flat, expecting that his son would care for his mother, Mr Tan’s wife.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: After he passed away, Mrs Tan continues to stay in the flat with her son and family, but is treated as non-existent by her son and family as far as they are concerned.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: She sleeps in the living room and cooks porridge for herself, whilst her son, daughter-in-law and grandchildren enjoy sumptuous meals.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The other two children meanwhile are estranged from Mrs Tan due to the "unfairness" of the flat having been favoured to their eldest brother.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The second story: Mr and Mrs Lee worked hard to bring up their only daughter.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: When she was about to be married, they sold their HDB flat, gave the proceeds to their daughter so that she might buy her own flat.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The understanding was that they would move in to stay with her.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Things did not work out as planned and they are now left homeless.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Stories, such as the above, abound and we may simply change surnames, number of children and permutations.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But the result is the same: parents part with their properties, their sale proceeds, their savings, only to be left with nothing, not even provision from their children.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Many of these parents may not wish to initiate any proceedings under the MPA.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Some of them may not even be eligible under the MPA.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But all of us can see the injustice and inequity in such situations.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The children have taken their parents’ property and left them bereft.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is irresponsible, cruel, unthinkable, but it happens, and often, too.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The law as it now stands is against the parent.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I speak with particular reference to cases where property is transferred or given by a parent to his or her child.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The current situation is that parents do not have much of a recourse.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: When we think that we give a property to our children for them to look after us, we think we can have it back.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But the legal position is that once we transfer the property, we cannot take it back, especially if we are a parent transferring the property to a son or a daughter.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The law presumes that it is meant as a gift and this is known as the presumption of advancement.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The burden falls on the parent to rebut the presumption.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, there are exceptions, such as trust, fraud, undue influence.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In each case, the evidentiary burden on parents is extremely high.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, adducing evidence may involve other family members and widen the family dispute, which is not at all to be encouraged.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The law as it stands also does not take into consideration changes in circumstances, such as where a child has a change of heart towards his or her parent after receiving the property.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, they are left to suffer in silence.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But ultimately, someone has to look after them, right?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And here is where the state steps in.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We can all see the unjustness in the situation.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, I urge the Government to consider reviewing the law to supplement the MPA and to seriously consider the following.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We are faced with vulnerable seniors, mostly with only one HDB flat, not landed gentry.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: These are vulnerable people who give their property to their children, children who then neglect, abuse or abandon them.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Second, we should legislate conditions under which a trust in favour of a parent can arise or must arise by operation of law, such as where an elderly parent transfers a substantial portion of his or her property to an adult son or daughter so that such son or daughter will hold property in trust for the parent.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This could apply when the transfer cannot be faulted.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I do note that there are areas of overlap and potential conflicts between the above measures that I have suggested.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We can and should rationalise and implement the measures holistically to form a robust framework to support seniors and reduce familial strain attributable to money matters.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I am also well aware that enforcement will be difficult since we are dealing with family relationships.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But we put the cart before the horse if we say enforcement must be achievable before we can set up a framework.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Tell that to an elderly person: I will not give you the right to take back your property because you may not be able to take it back anyway.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Can we say that to an elderly person?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is as good as a doctor telling his patient "I will not give you any option for a particular treatment unless I am sure it will work 100%".

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I do not think doctors will say that and I do not think that this House should be swayed by any argument that we should not have a framework unless we can ensure enforcement.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We need to set our moral and legal principles right and the rest will follow.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I wish to emphasise that I do not advocate that we legislate filial piety or, worse still, replace it.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Fundamentally, the responsibility, the privilege, remains with the family.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If I may quote Prof Walter Woon in response to any concern that my proposals could be too interventionist.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill is aimed at that recalcitrant small minority that cannot be counted on to do what is right, and therefore it will not affect the vast majority of Singaporeans.” So, Mr Deputy Speaker, my proposals are “aimed at that recalcitrant small minority that cannot be counted on to do what is right”.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, other Singaporeans have to pay for that failure.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It becomes an additional expenditure of public funds which could have been diverted to support those who are truly without family, and for other national purposes.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Not just a matter of public funds expenditure, such cruel and reprehensible behaviour, if left unaddressed, will immunise our people against basic human values.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It will immunise our children and set the tone for what our children, and society, will become.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It will immunise us against responsibility, suffering, justice and equity.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: What is now unacceptable will soon be common landscape, the way life is.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: What is now reprehensible becomes our lifestyle, the way we are.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The family unit will be threatened, our social fabric will tear.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We need to set our moral and legal principles right.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Otherwise, we fail miserably as a Government and society.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: On that note, Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is an inescapable fact of the human condition.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But it is a fact that we, human beings, all too often try to escape or decry or deny or despair of rather than embrace ageing as the doorway to a new different exciting phase of life with its own potential and pitfalls and this goes to the heart of the matter.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Archaeologists have found extremely ancient human skeletal remains where skeletons were obviously people who lived to a very old age, beyond the point when they could meaningfully contribute economically and where they may well have been invalid or immobile due to the kinds of illnesses that were rife in ancient times.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And yet they lived till they were very old.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The ancient tribes they lived within probably tended to them, helped to move from campsite to campsite, helped feed, clothe and care for them to enable them to live so long.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Embracing ageing and the aged defines a part of what it means to be human.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whether and how we include older people as equal members of our society is a mark of civilisation and humanity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On this barometer, I know that Singapore will never fall short.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In our homes, our workplaces or coffee shops, when Singaporeans speak of seniors who are their relatives, seniors who are their mentors, seniors that they know in their neighbourhoods or communities, it is inevitably in tones of respect, concern and empathy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This gut reaction speaks volumes about the kind of people Singaporeans are.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We defend those who are disadvantaged, even if they are frail and economically weak.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have an instinctive sense of social justice and fairness.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ancient human societies greatly valued older people because they had, to use a modern expression from the business world, racked up the air miles.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They had experienced many seasons, many cycles, many events and had a repository of memories of our natural conditions, interactions with other societies or tribes and intra-community dynamics that could add value to their communities and maybe even make the difference between life and death.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And yet in our modern societies, this logic is often turned on its head.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Older people are sometimes stigmatised and stereotyped as stuck in the mud, unable to keep up with the times, incapable of using technology, in short, as irrelevant.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am reminded of the time when a very old cashier at the shop once started a deep conversation with me.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At first, I instinctively got a little impatient.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A part of me said, "Oh, no, here comes a rambling senior, how can I extricate myself from this?" And then I thought while I get many calls, emails, visits today, every day as we all do, I think as Members of this House, a day may come when no one wants to talk to me.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I listened and I listened, and when I opened my mind, my heart, I realised that this lady had many interesting and useful insights, much wisdom to share.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After a while, I almost wanted to whip up my mobile device and start taking down notes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My unconscious bias had held me back from learning from, from being inspired by this person.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yes, older people do have a lot to contribute.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have to build a society that recognises, pools and embraces those contributions but we also have to build a society where older people have the confidence to make those contributions, to master enabling technologies and to speak to make their voice heard.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The rest of my speech, Sir, will touch on some of the broad principles we need to entrench in order to be a truly inclusive non-ageist society for the betterment of our soul.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will speak of these principles each in the form of a question.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moreover, many seniors will choose to work for intrinsic reasons if they could find the work options suited to their situation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of course, we should, because this means dignity for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More choices also mean more likelihood that seniors will choose to work in the way that suits them, thus raising labour force participation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we do more to unlock the benefits of technology and automation for seniors?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The concept of a social impact bond is something I have spoken about in the House previously.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Technology holds up the promise of better enabling seniors to lead productive lives, to contribute to the world of work in the way they feel best abled to and for longer.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The march of technology can also mitigate some of the ravages of age that might otherwise impede that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many seniors have a wealth of knowledge and experience but many may want to work in a part-time advisory or consulting capacity if those capacities existed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we do more to create platforms where seniors can contribute in a flexible way towards projects or to employers?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, there are platforms right now that match potential board members to board openings in the for-profit and not-for-profit sectors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Not every senior, of course, has the background to serve as a board member but many have pools of experience and niche skills to impart.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can create matching platforms for consulting freelance or part-time work.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Once again, NGOs will probably serve this role best and the Government can nudge and support these initiatives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Examples of success can be highlighted in marketing campaigns.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, can we do more to empower seniors to impart their experience?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to do more to nudge seniors to reskill their experience into a form where it can be usefully conveyed as training or consulting.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Experience is nothing if one does not process the experience and convert it into a form that is useful to others and to oneself.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One of my favourite quotes is from Aldous Huxley when he said, "Experience is not what happens to you; it is what you do with what happens to you".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should find ways to nudge our seniors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, using the SkillsFuture platform which has courses for trainers like the Advanced Certificate in Training and Assessment (ACTA) to reflect on their experience and be adept at converting this into forms that are useful, such as training videos, knowledge pills, podcasts and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fourthly, should we strive for non-discriminatory workplaces and social conditions?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Discrimination in all its forms is not just morally wrong.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It hurts our labour force participation and hurts the economy, meaning it hurts us all.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The fifth question is how to age with quality of life.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we do more to experiment with new platforms for delivering preventive healthcare into homes using telemedicine and artificial intelligence (AI), for example?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A last question is on the living environment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How do we build a good enabling living environment that gives older people the confidence to venture out, work part-time and get more socially engaged, knowing that at home, their basic needs are taken care of?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As with persons with disabilities, for older people, they would not be so disadvantaged, were it not for an urban environment not designed primarily with their needs in mind.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we do more to experiment with different models of living environment for older people beyond living by themselves or with their children, such as what they call assisted living in the United States (US), or what they call Silver Towns in Korea?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Silver Towns in Korea are towns which are comprehensive retirement communities, for example, in some cases, with facilities for young children to encourage frequent family visitations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And there is a variety of these Silver Towns catering to different income levels.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At this point, I declare that I am the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of an international research consultancy whose Korean arm has undertaken research into this field in Korea.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do we choose a Singapore where seniors are equal citizens, crucially engaged in society and playing a vital role by imparting their experience, their skills and wisdom and their inspiring example?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Or will we choose a future where seniors are, at worst, ignored or patronised or, at best, treated as a necessary evil, a politically significant constituency which should be shunted out of the mainstream but which should be mollified for other ends?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The choice needs to be made by us as a society, and it needs to be made by us as individuals, employers, employees, family members, commuters, residents and citizens.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On this question, we need a multi-pronged whole-of-Government and whole-of-society approach.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The difference we will make with this choice is profound and I have no doubt that Singapore and Singaporeans have always stood and will always stand on the right side of this question.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: These are common wishes of many seniors as they age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But the irony of ageing is that everyone wants to live as long as possible, and yet, also do not want to live too long because of the various aches and indignities that old age brings.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Personally, I feel we need to view this in a positive light.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Ageing may be inevitable, but the key is to understand the process and identify situations early, thereby enabling us to take preventive actions and decide how we wish to age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is never too early to ask ourselves what we must do to achieve this.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Also, these screenings can now be done at the polyclinics and regular general practitioner (GP) clinics.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This move is an encouraging step for many seniors and has been well-received.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Many seniors whom I met in Fengshan have told me that they have since undergone their health screening.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Follow-through actions post-health screening is another key area that is neglected by many seniors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We need to encourage them to understand how to better care or improve their conditions in certain areas.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In Fengshan, we are thankful for the support of MOH in establishing the Community Health Post for this purpose.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Now, our seniors can have individual coaching sessions from the healthcare professionals to take charge of their health and improve on it.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While these efforts are laudable, they are not preventive.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The way for preventive action is, of course, to maintain a healthy and active state from young.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Since last July, we have worked with the Health Promotion Board (HPB) and Active SG to introduce weekly exercises within the neighbourhood.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: My residents are excited with the variety of exercises that are available every day, from Mondays through Sundays.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Our young working adults now can also enjoy and exercise with us.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: And for the retirees and seniors, there are day exercises for them, too.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Seeing our seniors, working adults, children and grandchildren all in tow participating, I am cheered by the overwhelming response.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This is a headstart for our busy, working adults and it is actually a good start for the journey.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I remember one of the residents who told me that she is glad to be on this journey with us now.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: She said, "It is best to do so before one's body becomes stiff and weakens.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: When a person is affected by illness, even the most willing heart will be demotivated to exercise." And I totally agree with her.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: My concern is: will HPB or Active SG continue these in a long run?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Are there sufficient trainers to conduct these sessions?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I urge MOH to consider supporting and enhancing this great initiative.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: MOH can consider collaborating with the People's Association (PA), private organisations and freelancers or to train community interest groups in order to sustain a wider pool of trainers for the future.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While these sessions are free of charge, the impact it has on the community and country will be lasting.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Furthermore, funding such initiatives will come at a small price, compared to the subsidies that are required for the medical bills and also more medical infrastructural expansion.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Apart from health programmes, community involvement is pertinent for broader awareness outreach and having our seniors to be constantly engaged.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I trust that we are doing so in different ways on the ground and will further enhance these areas over time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Meanwhile, let me raise four aspects related to ageing that I would like to highlight for the Ministries to review.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I understand the current position is to decide the appeals on usage on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, I would like to ask MOH to reconsider and put in place a rule for a higher utilisation limit for those seniors who fulfil BHS in their MediSave and/or Minimum Sum in their Retirement Account (RA), particularly if they do not use this for their annual scans or diagnostics.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: During my house visits and dialogue sessions, seniors have expressed the same request to use more of their MediSave funds for the outpatient medical fees instead of using their cash or their spouse's to up their funds as they are also elderly.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Take the example of a 73-year-old resident of mine who is diabetic and has a heart condition.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: He shared that he needs to be on permanent medication to manage his health condition.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: By simple mathematics, he recounts that his MediSave funds will way outlive him.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Instead, the larger risk for him is when he cannot afford the regular medication to manage his conditions and thus result in complications.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To him, his MediSave funds will be worthless if he dies from diabetes or heart attack.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For chronic patients like him, I think being able to use their funds freely and at ease will be a huge relief as they need not worry about the cash outlay for requisite medications that sustain their lives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Second, to promote and encourage seniors to make an LPA by age 55.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Early protection is beneficial to both the seniors and their caregivers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Everyone would wish to live their lives in their preferred way and be given a choice.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We should maximise this opportunity to bring the LPA certificate issuers together with the community as we are concurrently doing outreach and communicating about elderly programmes or schemes to seniors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This will be useful for many seniors, especially in Singapore, where couples are usually co-owners of their property.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It can prevent situations where the elderly wish to downgrade or monetise their property to support expenses but are unable to do so due to the mental state of their spouse.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Similarly, an LPA will allow the seniors to decide in advance on their preferred palliative care if they do require it someday.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Respite care today is scarce and relatively high in cost.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We would hope that care support begins with the family and each would play their part and make the effort to provide the needful relief for the caregiver.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While the thought is good, caregivers, in reality, face different challenges even in their keenest desire of taking a break.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Many say this is where community involvement should begin.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Yes, to the extent that we can find community befrienders and match them to provide relief for caregivers and give them some time off.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: No, as there are other considerations that need to be in place.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: One example is how do we protect the befrienders and the beneficiary, as the person to be cared for has a different engagement and mental state?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Can the families entrust their loved ones and the home to a stranger for a period of time?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: What is the basis of understanding on the tasks that a befriender is supposed to undertake or, for that matter, not to be taken advantage of?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Once a month, make the centres available on a Saturday or Sunday for those caregivers who wish to place their seniors for a few hours at these centres.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: At the same time, we can introduce community befrienders to these centres.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With the presence and support of the centres’ trained professionals, the befrienders can help to care for the seniors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This would be a known, safer environment and provide assurance for all the parties.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We can also consider having a caregiver support network at the same location to give caregivers the opportunity to share experiences, talk amongst themselves or even offer free volunteer care services like hair service, massage, healthy meals prepared for these caregivers, who usually have no time for themselves.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Another option is to manage this through a knowledge-based approach and central management system to match the needs, to work with nursing homes or day care centres to provide respite care for a few hours at subsidised rates.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I ask that MOH consider the subsidies not only by household means testing, but to include consideration for whether alternative affordable caregiver option is, indeed, available, given today’s smaller family units.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Lastly, conscious planning and integration of housing with senior friendly infrastructure.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
