text: This can only happen with conscious planning, both infrastructures and programmes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We need to consider integrating housing for seniors within the community.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Back in 2016, together with the PAP Women’s Wing, we made a study trip to Hong Kong.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: One of the projects we viewed was an area where the public housing flats of seniors’ studio apartments were integrated with the regular public housing of 2- and 3-room flats for the seniors staying on the same floor, within the same building.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This makes it less of a retirement village and enables the elderly to be constantly engaged by immediate neighbours with younger families living nearby.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This can enable three-generation families to purchase units next to one another and encourage stronger family units or allow better social mix where the younger families can look out for the seniors next door.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I also encourage MND to plan having town audits throughout Singapore to ensure that the basic amenities and designs fulfil the needs to support an ageing population.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For the mature estates, to consider giving guidance on how we can better refit the amenities to suit the growing needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This will be beneficial in the long haul and save substantial spending when the final designs are constantly constructed with a senior-friendly state in mind.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In closing, Mr Deputy Speaker, I want to draw reference to a book titled "The Colours of Ageing" by Prof Kua Ee Heok.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The "Colours" in his book’s title represents the hope, will and the imagination of an "undefeated mind", which is, in my view, as crucial, if not more, to living with one’s faculties intact.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With our rapidly ageing population and longer life expectancies, it is important that we strive to help our seniors live a good quality of life for as long as possible.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These should be years in good mental, physical and emotional health during which they will be free to work productively and outside their interests.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our Government has been encouraging Singaporeans to lead healthy lifestyles to build up a strong foundation for their senior years.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We help Singaporeans monitor their health through very affordable health screenings.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How can we encourage more to go for screening and follow-up if found to have some unfavourable results?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Good health translates to a better quality of life.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The seniors who are in good health will be able to do pretty much everything that they used to when they were younger, to walk, eat, travel, socialise and take part in various activities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should have a public education about the appropriate exercises and diets best suited for the seniors.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To do this, we need differentiated platforms to engage them effectively.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can we introduce programmes targeting common illnesses among the elderly?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, for diabetic patients, what exercises are best for them?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How can these exercises help to lower blood sugar and weight?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These exercises can be illustrated on a chart and distributed to them so that they can do the exercises at home.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The mental health of our seniors is another area of concern.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We will have to raise public awareness and social acceptance of seniors with mental health issues to enable early detection and treatment.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I look forward to seeing the number of dementia-friendly communities like Yishun and MacPherson increase.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We can look at how to allow seniors with dementia to age in place as it can reduce the stress on them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, the name of the scheme "ElderShield" seems incompatible.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If our seniors desire, they can and should continue to work.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should not always think that our elderly cannot catch up.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While there will be individuals who experience greater challenges, we must also see them as progressive and willing to embrace lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are many shining examples in every sector and industry.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the latter mindset, we will realise that our seniors are people who can still contribute to our economy and make their mark in society.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, there was an 81-year-old nurse who was featured in the Straits Times last year.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are many like her in my constituency in Henderson-Dawson still going very strong.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is good to see them progress, too.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such seniors should be lauded for their care towards others, and the Government should work out a scheme to help them advance in their passions and careers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that, eventually, age will no longer be a consideration and we focus on an employee’s capability.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many seniors had told me that they feel left behind in our environment of rapid digitalisation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They are especially uncomfortable with the initiatives to go cashless.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many are so used to the passbook to monitor their debit and credit that the electronic bank statement, to them, is a problem.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Communications via applications, such as WhatsApp and emails, going online to obtain information and perform transactions, are not easily grasped by a significant portion of our seniors.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Part of the reason is the language gap.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of our seniors are not literate or fluent in English.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If there are applications and websites in mother tongues, such as Chinese and Malay, I believe it would help tremendously.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are physiological problems when they use smartphones.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The font sizes are small and it is not easy for elderly persons to read the small text and to scroll up and down.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Navigating the various icons to get to what they want is a challenge.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many complained that the touchscreens do not respond well to their drier fingertips, and pain in their finger joints is another problem.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Twenty years ago, there were some resistance to automated teller machines (ATMs).

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This was because these machines pose fewer physical challenges.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And very importantly, these big installations can be trusted because they have been set up by banks.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the other hand, transactions on smartphones or online are unsettling to our seniors because they are not quite sure if their monies are flowing to the right accounts or parties.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Frequent news about scams online also make them very nervous.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have to address all our seniors’ concerns through holistic measures, customised education and familiarisation programmes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: More of our seniors should be encouraged to volunteer as part of active ageing.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is an activity which allows the elderly to stay engaged in the community and derive a sense of satisfaction from giving back and, in turn, enable the community to tap upon their wisdom and years of rich experience.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Research has also shown that the elderly who have meaningful relationships and are engaged in their communities are happier and healthier.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Volunteering gives them a deep sense of purpose.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, getting our seniors to volunteer on a sustainable basis may not be easy.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It can be extended later to include other parties, including individuals, through platforms which allow bartering of services.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition to recruiting and attracting seniors, we should also design programmes such that our younger generation can be involved.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is useful and helpful because it brings together Pioneer Generation ambassadors to coordinate various support services for senior citizens.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It also provides an opportunity for seniors to volunteer, with 40% of the ambassadors aged 60 and above.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Volunteers can play a big role to engage the socially isolated elderly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In reaching out to them, they not only bring light and warmth to them, but they also assist beleaguered families and relieve caregivers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Due to the increasing number of those ageing and those who will be isolated when they become less mobile, it is not feasible to just depend on trained personnel.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The community must be involved to complement the reach of social workers and medical health workers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Initiatives that organise neighbours, volunteers and activists to be befrienders and to reach out to the socially isolated seniors are beneficial to our elderly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When we visit them regularly, we keep them engaged and tend to their emotional well-being.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We are also more likely to find out about their issues early and deal with their healthcare and emotional concerns early.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such initiatives strengthen neighbourliness, as we actively look out for one another.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are already initiatives to provide more support to caregivers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, with smaller family sizes and more double-income households, it is inevitable that, increasingly, families will have to entrust the important responsibility of caregiving to professionals.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have no alternative but to continue work on boosting the capability and capacity of our professional caregiving sector.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: MOH is tapping on retired nurses, who can be re-engaged on a casual basis.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Building up this network of retired medical professionals will complement what our healthcare community can offer.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would be very much appreciated for family emergencies involving the elderly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Lastly, I want to touch on physical accessibility for all seniors.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They should be "flats-for-life" – accessible to the elderly which, incidentally, would also be accessible for the disabled and families with young children.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Floors should be levelled, switches and sockets repositioned, doors, bathrooms and toilets should be widened to enable wheelchair movements.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For our public transport, I hope directional signs and notices have bigger fonts against high contrast backgrounds to make them easier to read.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Thanks to the efforts of our elders, we reap the fruits of their labour.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Let us work together to provide them with the best care they deserve in their golden years.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I conclude with my support for the Motion, Sir.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   First of all, I would like to thank the Members who moved the Motion.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: My speech today is based on my personal experience, what I experienced through my work in the arts, as well as my encounters with many senior citizens.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: When he was young, he devoted his life to work in order to support our family.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Like many "traditional" fathers of that era, he was strict and reserved and was not particularly close to his children.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Deputy Speaker, can I take a break first, and let the other Members speak first?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Deputy Speaker, if I may first speak in Mandarin and then in English.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the Motion today.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Three years ago, we celebrated SG50 and, once again, confirmed the contributions of our Pioneer Generation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Undoubtedly, it is their contributions and sacrifices that have brought about the achievements we have today.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, respecting and appreciating the elderly is a matter of course.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, respecting and appreciating the elderly require not just words but actions, too.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Much of the infrastructure that we have today was built in a different era when our population was still young.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In a rapidly-ageing environment today, we must make adjustments to ensure that the elderly can remain physically and mentally active and age in place gracefully.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government has done a lot in this area.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many of our colleagues have made various good suggestions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, we should apply elderly-friendly designs into our hardware and heartware solutions in all aspects of life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Success of any innovation depends on the design.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, we must use technology and AI to supplement our shortage of manpower, so that more senior citizens, including those who live alone and are less mobile, can age in place and live independently.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Third, we must strengthen our community service organisations, optimise the allocation of resources and manpower, and encourage more people to volunteer in the community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: By doing this, we can not only solve the manpower shortage problem but also demonstrate a human touch.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must change the negative mindset that "as people age, they become useless".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Each age group has its own set of issues, and we all need to be more tolerant and learn to adjust.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: When we grow old, we may become weaker physically, but we are wiser.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As long as we make the necessary adjustments, we can live a fulfilling and colourful life in old age.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We hope the Government can take the lead to create an elderly-friendly work environment and set out human resource (HR) policies that are suitable for mature workers, so that seniors who love working and want to continue to work, can continue to make meaningful contributions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: More importantly, we should encourage the elderly to remain positive and active both physically and mentally, so that they can lead a more meaningful life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In English): Our seniors dedicated the prime years of their lives to build the Singapore we are so proud of today.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They deserve our respect and we should certainly honour them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Honouring them requires not just words but actions, too.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Much of what we have today, including the hardware and social infrastructure, was designed decades ago when our population was still young.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is time to refresh these to welcome a different population landscape with a different set of requirements.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With Singapore undergoing rapid ageing, it is important that we set the right policies, put in the right resources and organise ourselves better in the right way sooner than later.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to ensure adequate support for our elderly today and tomorrow, so that we are all empowered to age gracefully and actively in the comfort of our own homes and communities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This Government has increased social spending and will continue to spend more.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must enable our elderly today and tomorrow to continue leading an independent and graceful life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There are three recommendations that I would like to put forth in the hope of enabling our seniors’ daily lives better.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First is to apply elderly-friendly designs into our hardware and heartware solutions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must ensure that all our designs are designs for inclusion.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We should not take the easy way out, or for the sake of efficiency and design only for that 80%, which would then lead to exclusion, which is definitely an outcome that we wish not to see.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Currently, there are only two silver industry guidelines in Singapore – "Guidelines for age-friendly homes" and "Guidance for digital devices and online services to be senior friendly".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These are a good start, but we need to mainstream elderly-friendly designs much more and make them pervasive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to apply elderly-friendly designs to the development of common spaces, facilities, machine and software interfaces, workflows, public processes and more.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We could create specialisations for students to undertake in tertiary institutions, so that we build up a supply of talent with the expertise.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We could also set up a Government department that does research, set standards and audit public and private projects to ensure elderly-friendliness.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, proliferate digital eldercare to supplement the shortage of manpower.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There may soon be a point in time when there are more who need care than those who can care.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: By leveraging technology and AI more effectively, we can drastically change how care is provided and help even more Singaporeans to age in place.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Japan is even further ahead of us in terms of ageing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They have an increasing number of elderly with a decreasing number of working adults.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They suffer severe labour shortage, especially in eldercare nursing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Yet, they reinvented how the elderly can be cared for by leveraging technology and AI.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: From Toyota’s Robina and Humanoid, Honda’s ASIMO, Tokai’s Robot for Interactive Body Assistance (RIBA) to the National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology's (AIST’s) Puppets for Animal Therapy (PARO), Japan has a full range of robots that can help the elderly with household chores, get out of bed, conduct conversations complete with emotions, and even help paraplegics to walk again.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Imagine if these solutions are available to us in Singapore, many elderly, whom we used to think can only be cared for in nursing homes, can now lead a fairly independent life in the comfort of their own HDB flats.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Alas, while these are all possible, it is still not known if these solutions can be exported and at what price.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Could the Government share some of the success cases so far?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Could we accelerate developments locally and implement them sooner than later?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Relying on salaried staff is not enough and, despite my strong support for digital eldercare, I do also believe that the human touch is still very much needed and cannot be replaced.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need more Singaporeans to step in and step up to help.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We can leave the professional part of caring of the elderly to the salaried staff and AI robots.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But there are many opportunities for volunteers to step in.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, accompany the elderly to medical appointments, give them a ride to hospitals, clean their homes, deliver groceries or just offer a listening ear.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There are kind souls already helping in these areas, but the need is far higher than the supply of volunteers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, we need to find ways to involve more Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Assuming a population of about 30,000 in a constituency, with a third being elderly, a third being adults and another third being minors, if the adults can just spare two hours every week, we will have more than 20,000 hours of help available in any week.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Scale it across Singapore, we will have millions of volunteer hours available, and so much can be achieved.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But I also believe that we need to be more ambitious than this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We should aspire to having all Singaporeans do community service and on a long-term sustainable basis.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If each person could just spare one to two hours per week engaging in a specific volunteer "vocation" with clear roles and responsibilities spelt out, we can achieve a lot more.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Today, we have a myriad of formal and informal groups of volunteer organisations doing community service, serving from their hearts.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We have seen passionate Singaporeans, young and old, dedicating days of their weeks serving the less fortunate.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Still, we also see Singaporeans who would like to serve but are unsure of what they can do, what needs are still unfulfilled and whether the time commitment will be too great for them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, we need to find ways to make serving a priority and organise ourselves better so that busy Singaporeans can just "plug and play" when serving the community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At present, SG Cares is perhaps the best place to play this role but it will need a clear structure, concrete programmes and strong support to do so.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I hope Singaporeans will see community service as a priority in life and respond to the call to get involved in a bigger way for a more sustainable future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As we enhance our healthcare, we can expect longer and more healthy years.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As our economy evolves, there will be less reliance on physical strength at the workplace but more use of intellect and wisdom.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As each population becomes better educated and more savvy with the digital space, there will be less fear and deeper entrenchment of technology in our lives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some hold the belief that, in Chinese, "老了不中用", which means that you become useless as you age.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: While I understand that there are some constraints that come with age, I do not agree with this belief.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is self-defeating and we risk a self-fulfilling prophecy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to keep active and keep trying.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We have seen elderly in their 90s who remain active and sharp, even learning a new language.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Of course, we hope we do not have to work into our old age because we have to, but because we love to.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It helps us to look forward to every new day.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, we should do three things to help our seniors keep active and continue to do well in their old age.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, create a favourable environment and employment opportunities for seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Pioneer Generation Ambassador is a wonderful programme.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Make it easy and inexcusable for everyone to keep fit and stay social.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Ultimately, we need to transform our culture and mindsets.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Every Singaporean needs to believe that we each have a role to play beyond our family and employment obligations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to recognise that it is not enough to rely on salaried staff because they are financially obliged to carry out the care.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A caring and inclusive society cannot be one that the citizens only talk about it and expect someone else to do it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I believe that seniors are a gift to our society.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I will continue from where I left off.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: He would forget what my mother told him despite having asked about it repeatedly, and his temper also flared more easily.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: To comfort him and also ourselves, we told him that he was just getting old.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: What exactly does it mean to "become old"?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: There is a word which is used together with the word "lao" (old) and that word is "shuai" (to be weakened).

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Put together, "shuai lao" means old and weakened.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: These two words create a very negative attitude towards ageing.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: There are many of these words but, to summarise in Hokkien, it is simply "suay" (unfortunate).

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Many people refuse to think about the stage of our lives where we age and then die.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Perhaps you will think about your retirement, perhaps you will start to do some financial planning, but to really understand the process of ageing is something that all of us want to avoid.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Perhaps, we should have realised this fact of life much earlier – birth, sickness, ageing and dying are all essential parts of life.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: We cannot just pay attention to living, but we need to also understand ageing and the process of dying.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: We must accept that our healthy bodies will eventually become weak and our sharp minds will one day become slow.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Things that we used to do easily may become challenging.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: You may not be able to button your shirt; going to the toilet becomes inconvenient; you may need help in the morning.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: And what is most humiliating is that you may have to put on diapers.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: All these inconveniences and situations can slowly erode the will of a person who used to be full of life and ideals.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Over time, he may find that he can no longer face others nor look at himself with dignity, and he begins to feel helpless, fearful and lonely.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Looking back at my father's bouts of anger back then, as his son, I did not notice his helplessness, fear and loneliness.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Through this process, I begin to wonder: have we understood the process of ageing and dying?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: If we have a better understanding of ageing and dying, we may be able to help the elderly around us handle the process.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Our society must start to pay attention to this and learn to accept and prepare for ageing, as an individual and as a community.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Why is this society always celebrating life, celebrating the birth of a child but not paying attention to the process of ageing and dying?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: A human being’s existence should not be measured in terms of how much wealth he has created but how he has lived every stage of his life with dignity.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: If I was closer to my father, perhaps I would have noticed the problems earlier.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: For the first group, I think we can still help them if they have friends and relatives.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: However, for the second and third groups, namely, those who are on bad terms with their friends and relatives and those who are not in touch with their kin, their twilight years tend to be difficult.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: There was one occasion when we organised a seminar on the issue of wills, and many elderly folks rushed to ask the lawyers many questions.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: However, all the questions were basically about this – "Mr Lawyer, what do you think if I allocate my assets this way?" The lawyers felt perplexed, "Why do they ask my views on how they want to divide their assets?" After several rounds of discussions, I realised that all of them were worried that their family members would feel aggrieved about how the assets were distributed.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: In fact, the fundamental problem was that they had proceeded with the will without settling their family problems first.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: A Filipino nurse whom I interviewed before, told me that she was puzzled by what she saw when she started working in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Through the experience she shared, we know that if an elderly family member falls ill, he would not be afraid, as he knows that those around him and those who are close to him will look after him and support him.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Many people will say that it is not easy to do that in Singapore, especially when most of our families are small families and there are few siblings whom we can share the burden of caregiving with.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Moreover, faced with daily stress and long working hours, they can only choose to depend on domestic helpers in the end.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Further, I often see that the caregivers of the elderly are also around the same age as them.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: So, can you imagine an elderly person looking after another elderly person?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: My mother says she always believed that she would become a burden to her children.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Actually, I am quite worried about whether young people know how to look after their elderly family members, because many young parents today do not even look after their own children.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Instead, they leave their kids to their parents or domestic helpers.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: However, looking after your loved ones brings a lot of joy.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I remember helping my father change his diapers and bathe for the first time.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: These experiences left a very deep impression on me.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: These intimate contacts with my father helped me understand the physical changes he experienced through the process of falling ill and ageing.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: When I took him to see the doctor, kept him company at the hospital and fed him, my relationship with him improved.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Previously, my father seldom smiled at me, but now, he always smiles when he sees me.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Through this process, I learnt to think from the other person’s perspective and understood what empathy means, because when you look after a patient and an elderly person, you must look at things from their perspective.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: To enable the elderly to live their twilight years with dignity, we must create an environment where they feel secure, and that begins with ourselves.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: When I was drafting this speech, this poem by Ma Zhiyuan kept ringing in my mind. "Dry vines, old trees, and a crow; a home by a small bridge and a flowing stream; a horse on the ancient path stands against the western wind; as the sun sets, a man roams the world, broken-hearted." Does life need to be so sad and lonely when one enters the withering season of fall?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many residents have lived there for 20 to 30 years, some with other family members living within the area.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Bukit Batok East is their kampung and most do not want to move out of the area.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I meet many elderly residents regularly at events, house visits and my MPS.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many elderly residents I meet at MPS have sought financial assistance to cope with their daily living expenses.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe my experience is no different from that of other Members.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some of these seniors have insufficient income or sources of funds to pay their bills, medical expenses or even food.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They may not meet the criteria to receive financial assistance because of the fact that they are working or have children who are expected to support them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In many cases, the seniors are reluctant to seek assistance from their children and the most common reason cited is that their children are having financial difficulties, too.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The children may also not truly appreciate the issues that their elderly parents are facing.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One of my residents shared with me that her children had scolded her when they found out that she sought financial assistance.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Instead of supporting her, they chided her and told her she needed to adjust her lifestyle.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Her lifestyle was by no means lavish, so she was hurt by her children's response.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She was crying when she told me that her son told her that if finances are so tight, she should just eat rice and soya sauce.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I acknowledge that not all of the residents fall into the category of needy beneficiaries but the reality is that day-to-day living is a challenge for them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It will not be feasible to expect financial assistance for all these families and I also believe that, to some extent, there must be personal and familial responsibility.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Therefore, the solution is not to give more money to more people.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I think that there is scope though to review the existing support structures in place to better assist seniors to cope with their financial challenges.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note the enhancements that have been made over the years and more seniors have now successfully applied for the scheme.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Could there be additional outreach to enhance awareness and acceptance amongst elderly residents?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is an ongoing call for the scheme to be extended to bigger flats.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note the indication from the Minister for National Development earlier this year that it is not likely to happen anytime soon as it is not an effective use of space and a more feasible option is to right-size.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I would ask, however, that the Ministry reconsider this view.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Ageing-in-place is a key component in ensuring an elderly person ages successfully with dignity.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Being able to continue staying where they are living has an impact on their mental and, therefore, also physical well-being.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At a practical level, there may be further costs and implications of having to move to a new location.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This scheme provides an opportunity to alleviate the elderly from their financial challenges.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If this scheme is extended, more can benefit from it.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: That means more elderly residents have the chance to improve their financial situation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In respect of outreach, there is awareness of the existence of the scheme.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, there is still some resistance to it.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The family home is seen as sacred and many fear the implications of outliving the lease period or not leaving anything as inheritance to their children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I feel though that given that more Singaporeans are asset-rich rather than cash-rich, an equity release product like this is an effective measure to meet the elderly's financial needs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It may, therefore, be worth the effort to generate more acceptance of this scheme.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: CHAS enables Singapore Citizens from lower- to middle-income households to receive subsidies for medical and dental care at participating general practitioner and dental clinics near their home.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Singapore Citizens who qualify receive an individual blue or orange CHAS card.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I often receive appeals to qualify for CHAS and for an "upgrade" to the blue card.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Typical issues that arise include the fact that an adult child is using the home address but not living there or living in the same address but is not contributing to the household expenses.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The elderly feel that they are unfairly assessed and deprived of the much sought after CHAS card.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One other proposal I would like to make is for a review of the role and branding of the Tribunal for the Maintenance of Parents.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This Tribunal was created as a means for parents to seek maintenance from their adult children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The work done by the Commissioner for the Maintenance of Parents and the Tribunal is not just adjudication though, as there is a lot of effort in conciliation and mediation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is, however, great resistance from the elderly when they are asked to approach the Commissioner or the Tribunal, as a prelude to an application for financial assistance.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At this juncture, I should just declare that I am also a mediator with the Tribunal for Maintenance of Parents.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many have approached me and explained that they are uncomfortable about pursuing claims from their children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I feel that there is scope for a review of efforts that could be done in educating the public about the family being the first line of defence and how the family can handle financial issues together.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I would propose that the role of the Tribunal be reviewed and enhanced to assist families beyond just adjudication and mediation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Perhaps there could be more services provided to the elderly and their family members, such as counselling or financial planning classes, akin to the extended support available to families in the Family Justice Courts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I move to the second issue of concern – mental wellness.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Through house visits and feedback from grassroots leaders, it has come to my attention that there are many seniors who are living alone and who may not participate in community activities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some may not have children or close relatives and end up being isolated.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are clearly undesirable effects of isolation, as we worry about the safety and well-being of the elderly.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Another important aspect though is the impact on their mental well-being.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Being disconnected with the world does not encourage active and healthy ageing.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The elderly may not always want help but I believe it is important to set up an ecosystem where the elderly feel connected to the community and can seek out assistance when necessary.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is a constant work in progress to reach out to the elderly residents.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I feel that we should continue to encourage neighbours and grassroots leaders to look out for and connect with the seniors.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is a meaningful endeavour which should be built on further.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This leads me to my last point relating to community support.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have many schemes and programmes in place but there will always be gaps and those who fall through the cracks.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe that the community plays an important role to complete the support structure for the elderly and close the gaps.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For example, in Bukit Batok East, some of the elderly residents who may not be eligible for financial assistance receive monthly food rations which had been donated by merchants, community partners and grassroots leaders.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Basically, patrons of the coffee shop are encouraged to buy an extra meal and these paid-for meals could then be redeemed by beneficiaries identified by the RC.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Although this scheme benefits all needy beneficiaries regardless of age, there is a high concentration of elderly residents in that area who will find this scheme meaningful and will benefit from it.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: My youth volunteers also follow up on many MPS cases involving elderly residents to ensure that there is closure and they receive the support that they need.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These are just some examples of organic support from within the community which helps to augment the schemes and services made available by the Government.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is important that ground-up initiatives are supported and encouraged so that we could build a better support structure for the elderly residents within our community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, allow me to say a few words in Malay.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   In the Malay language, we refer to the elderly as the golden group.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This obviously has a deep and meaningful connotation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Seniors are a group who should be appreciated and looked after well.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Today’s Motion calls on us to view the elderly as a gift to society, as a key asset.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many seniors are still working and contributing to their families and the national economy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If the seniors’ health are looked after and they stay active, they can certainly continue being the movers of the community and the nation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Therefore, it is important for us to update the current policies and schemes to ensure the well-being of our seniors are looked after.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In addition, it is also important for the general public to continue playing their role and complement the support given to the elderly.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am certain that, with a joint effort by the Government, families and the community, a comprehensive network of support can be established.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, I will conclude in English.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We need to take care of the elderly because it is the right thing to do.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But we should also remember that we will all grow old one day.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As more of our people age, it is necessary for us to support them in a holistic manner to ensure their physical, mental and emotional needs are well taken care of.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our current approach for healthcare, which is to focus on a healthy lifestyle for all, is the right one.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Healthy habits will contribute to better health in old age and reduce both physical and mental hardship for our seniors and their families.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The best and surest way to minimise medical expenditures is to live clean, exercise discipline in our food intake and adopt active lifestyles.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For our seniors, even if they had not had healthy habits before, it is never too late and we should support and encourage them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I appeal to the National Health Promotion Board (HPB) to step up its good work in public education, including reaching out to seniors through the mass media in their various vernacular.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is a need to ride on the success of homecare medical services and increase the number of such service points to increase the outreach of such services, in addition to the employment of skilled caretakers to meet the needs of our elderly.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is very important that we work together to ensure that such assisted living models be adapted to our local conditions and fit in with our HDB estate living settings, where the majority of Singaporeans are.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, there are still Singaporeans who do not quite understand how MediShield Life and other support schemes for the elderly work, despite the efforts of our volunteers, community and grassroots leaders, such as the Pioneer Generation (PG) Ambassadors.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At least for medical bills, the elderly can approach the medical social workers for details.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, if they require other forms of assistance, such as financial help or protection from abuse by those around them, ignorance may cost them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How then can we reach out to these pockets of seniors?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope we can take the time and effort to look into how we can reach pockets of elderly who need various types of assistance or protection, through public dialogues, consultations or formally appointing a committee to develop a feasible and durable framework to deal with this challenge.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The promotion of family values, especially the care of grandparents and parents, is a continuous effort and needs to be further deepened.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is a Chinese saying, "家 有 一 老 , 如 有 一 宝 ".

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It means that the elderly are like a treasure.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are cases where the children do not take the responsibility to take care of their parents and parents who choose to shield their children even when they do not do their duties or even ill-treat them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With smaller family size, the significance of families in unity would increase, especially when we are facing an ageing population.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need greater efforts in public education and should review our family mediation set-ups as well as legislative frameworks to address family conflicts involving the seniors or the elderly.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We also need to avoid placing excessive financial and care burdens on our children.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe, all Members would have come across this feedback from residents.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Most residents I spoke to do not wish to burden their children or grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With declining health, moving to a smaller home is more advisable.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But for those who insist on ageing-in-place, how they can monetise their homes is a perennial challenge.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As an aspiring Smart nation, we should pay attention to how increasing the use of technology could help enhance support services for our elderly.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Successful developments will go a long way to reducing the burdens on our young which is also the wish of our parents and our seniors.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, I would like to conclude with my support for the Motion.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is a timely one and I laud the efforts of my fellow Members of this House who filed this Motion.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In our frequent interactions with our residents, we have come across seniors or elderly residents who have lamented on the different challenges and issues they face, such as the lack of employment opportunities, being financially dependent, being neglected by their children or having strained familial relationships.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Viswa is a resident I have met several times at MPS.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: He is 70 years old and is married to his 68-year-old wife for more than 40 years.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They have one son in his 40s who is in prison.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Before their son was sent to prison, he financially supported both Mr Viswa and his wife.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Now that he is incarcerated, Mr Viswa and his wife have to fend for themselves.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Viswa is adamant that he must find a job to pay the bills and support his wife who has ailing health.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we try our best to give him some interim financial assistance and to get some form of employment assistance for Mr Viswa, jobs for someone his age are difficult to come by.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fortunately, after several months of appealing for employment assistance and employment opportunities, Mr Viswa was offered a part-time position.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While he is happy to have found employment, I am also worried if he will be alright and if he can continue in his job.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The reality is that with families getting smaller, we will end up having many elderly and seniors among us who may need to fend for themselves and continue to work into their golden years.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While this, in itself, is not a bad thing, so long as our seniors continue to keep healthy, fit and active, and continue to sharpen their skills, more than health or skills, they need opportunities to be employed and be entrusted with work responsibilities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They may not be able to carry out physically demanding work but they do have invaluable experience and knowledge that we can tap on.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, they can be assigned as workplace mentors to train younger workers or be tasked to do administrative or information organisation work that would require a fair amount of patience which, I am sure, they have more of, compared to younger counterparts.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the universities and some institutions of higher learning, professors and lecturers are given tenure until they are 65 years old ‒ what we call T65 ‒ which is proof that they are able to carry on teaching, writing, doing academic and research work until they are 65 years old.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For many of our seniors, they take pride in being financially independent and not having to ask their children or anyone else for financial assistance.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are some seniors who are in the fortunate position of being financially independent or being able to get financial support from their children or other family members, but there are others who are not so fortunate.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   Mdm Aminah is a senior citizen who is a rather petite lady.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: She is in her 60s and lives alone in a rental flat, even though she has an adult grandchild who is supposed to live with her.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although all of them are working, Mdm Aminah is a recipient of financial assistance from the Government.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have visited Mdm Aminah at her flat to give her some groceries and also to speak to her.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: From our conversations, I discovered that her children give her between $10 to $20 each month and take turns to visit her every weekend.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For most of the week, Mdm Aminah is all alone.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I asked her whether the money given by her children is sufficient.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The financial assistance that she receives from the Social Service Office (SSO) does help to reduce her financial burden slightly.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: She said that she does not want to burden or embarrass her children.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have also met Mr Mohamed and his wife who are both in their 60s, too.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They met me at the MPS and asked me to help them get a rental flat.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At that time, they were living with their son and his wife in their 5-room flat, but they were chased out of that flat.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When asked about the circumstances leading to this situation, I found out that Mr Mohamed and his wife sold their 3-room flat around 10 years earlier in order to help their son buy a bigger flat and gave the proceeds from the sale of their house to buy their son’s 5-room flat.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Now, after almost 10 years have passed, they were chased out of that same 5-room flat.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They were very worried and were scrambling to get a rental flat.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It was heart-wrenching for me to hear their story.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When I think of these two situations, I often asked myself where is the compassion and sympathy towards these elderly parents?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Why are some people so cruel to them?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These elderly parents willingly sacrificed their heart and soul for their children, but yet, why can their children not repay their sacrifice?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the proverb goes, the elderly have to tolerate all kinds of behaviour.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fortunately, there is a diligent effort by our volunteers to engage our seniors and offer much needed assistance.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nonetheless, the responsibility of taking care of our seniors falls primarily on each one of their children, and it should not be the main responsibility of society and the Government.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Parents are a gift and we should fulfil our obligations and look after them throughout their remaining years.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should never become like those who abandon their parents.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Madam Loh is a resident whom I met recently at MPS.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: She was in tears as she sought help to get a rental flat.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Like Mr Mohamed and his wife, Madam Loh lives with her son and daughter-in-law.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, their familial relationships were strained after living together for four years and Madam Loh was asked to leave the flat.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: She is desperately looking for a rental flat as she has no other children and does not wish to live with relatives, because she is embarrassed to let them know.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In her desperation, she said she wants to take her own life so that she need not be a burden to anyone anymore.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For each of these cases above, my heart breaks at the despair and sadness faced by each of these elderly persons.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Should that not be a responsibility that comes willingly from the heart?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should not be compelled to take care of our parents because the law says so.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should do it because it is the right thing to do.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is a topic that is especially close to my heart.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In my first General Election rally speech, I spoke about active ageing and what it meant for me personally and for my constituents.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I shared how I was inspired by my grandmother and my wish for our elderly to lead fulfilling lives after they retire, to carry on with pride and dignity.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is a primary driver for many of the programmes that I introduce for my residents in Tampines.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Its stated mission is to build active networks amongst the elderly, to actively engage the community and provide them with a path to seek help in times of need.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am glad that Tampines is selected to pilot the programme.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some told me they have made new friends and are enjoying their retirement.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: One Mr K, 82 years old, is less reliant on the wheelchair and uses his walking stick to come for classes.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Under the Community Network for Seniors (CNS), there is also Eastern Health Alliance’s Care Line Programme.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is a tele-befriending service targeting the elderly who stay alone or require a befriender.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But it is not just about isolated seniors.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Many of our seniors live with their children or near them.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Many people are unaware of the schemes available to them.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: House visits by PG Ambassadors really help to raise awareness and dispel some of their worries.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: So, CNS closes gaps and works closely with the local community to help residents.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There is a whole network of agencies from the Red Cross, St Andrews Community Hospital, Singhealth, Lion Befrienders, HPB, RCs and so on supporting this.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Jacelyn, aged 60, is passionate about line dancing and conducts free weekly classes in Tampines for about 60 residents.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There are many individuals out there who care about the community.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Let us tap on them, encourage them, motivate them.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: CNS is working well, and I read that it will be expanded to more areas soon.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I also suggested building eldercare and childcare centres in our parks and schools then.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I drew from our positive experience in our 3-in-1 Family Centre in Tampines which was set up in 1990, incorporating childcare, student care and eldercare.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: A couple of years ago, I learnt that there will be a new nursing home on Tampines Avenue 2 that is situated next to Angsana Primary School.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: When I saw the design of the nursing home, I advocated for the fence between the two buildings to be removed in order to remove physical barriers between the nursing home and the school.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I do not like the fenced-up feeling in nursing homes.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is uninviting and isolates them from the community.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I wanted the school field to be available to the nursing home for exercises and activities and also to make it convenient for parents and grandparents to drop in after dropping off their children in school.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It was in December 2015 that we saw the artist's impression and we are still waiting for an operator to be appointed and no ground breaking yet.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I know it is happening soon but I feel we need to move things faster.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, I am very encouraged by the commitment of our Government in preparing for an ageing population.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I note that the Inter-Ministerial Committee for Ageing was set up 20 years ago in 1998 to review healthcare needs of the elderly and to ensure that the healthcare cost remains affordable.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Since then, many policies, programmes and initiatives have been implemented and many more Ministries and agencies involved – active ageing under the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY), Pioneer Generation Office (PGO) under MOF, Ageing Planning Office under MOH, Silver Support Scheme under the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) and so on.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Much has been done, but I believe much more can and must be done.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For example, there are many exciting new technologies to assist the elderly, from wearable devices to remote monitoring.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can we do more to encourage this sector?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can we aspire to be a global leader in technology-assisted elderly living and active ageing?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Should we coordinate all the efforts and resources to see how we can make better use of our seniors' experience and wisdom?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: How do we tap on our retirees to continue to play active roles in the country that they have given so much to, and for them to live the rest of their lives in Singapore in a dignified and fruitful manner?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is also a complex one, and my remarks today do not fully express what I have to say on this topic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As the Chinese saying goes, a senior in the family is like a treasure in the family, or in Chinese, "家有一老，如有一宝".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We agree with Dr Lily Neo that our seniors are assets to our society and our country.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Our seniors are key pillars in families, as parents and grandparents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: They not only raise us but also educate and bring up grandchildren with the right values and traditions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Many of our seniors are also leaders in the community, contributing their wisdom to community development.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Today, more than one in three of our PG Ambassadors and around one in two of the HPB Health Ambassadors are over 60.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: At the economic level, many seniors are experienced business owners, while our silver workforce is also emerging as a key driver of our economic development, complementing a younger workforce that is likely to shrink in the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Our vision for Singapore is a "Nation for All Ages".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In particular, we want to deepen our efforts to achieve positive ageing at three levels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: First, at the individual level, we want to enable our citizens to continue to develop and grow as individuals, regardless of age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This includes enabling them to work for as long as they choose to.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In 2017, over 1,400 retired nurses aged above 62 were working, compared to 1,200 in 2015.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: MOH will continue to work with our healthcare institutions to support flexible work arrangements for older nurses, so that they can continue to contribute.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: At the same time, other seniors may seek purpose in their silver years, not by working but by developing their interests or pursuing their own passion or causes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Dr Lily Neo also suggested that the Government set up policies and programmes to promote volunteerism amongst seniors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To date, we have funded 22 volunteer programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: One such programme is the Community Befriending Programme (CBP), whereby the SVF provides programme funding to recruit, train and deploy active agers as befrienders to older seniors, including covering some out-of-pocket costs for these befrienders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We note Ms Joan Pereira’s suggestion and would be happy to explore time banking in future where there is ground-up interest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Confidence and purpose in our silver years are only possible with good health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We agree with Dr Lily Neo and Mr Gan Thiam Poh that the promotion of health and well-being of seniors is key.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have brought preventive health services to over 44,000 mature workers in seven sectors, and exercise programmes and health talks to over 400,000 seniors in the community to keep them in good health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Close to 25,000 Singaporeans aged 50 and above have attended screening under the programme in the last five months.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Second, at the family level, we want to empower caregivers to better support seniors to age in place with peace of mind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I agree with Miss Cheryl Chan, Mr Kok Heng Leun as well as Mr Gan Thiam Poh that caregiver support and strong families are critical.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Our efforts to enhance home and community care services are aimed at supporting seniors in the day, so that their caregivers can go to work with peace of mind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have worked to increase the capacity, improve on accessibility and also raise the quality of our services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In 2016, we started Integrated Home and Day Care packages, which give seniors flexibility to be cared for, either at the centres or at home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We are also building nursing homes in the community to support those who are too frail to be cared for at home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui said that she cannot wait.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I am sure it is worth waiting for.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Miss Cheng also spoke on improving the design and programming for our eldercare facilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We agree and have been injecting more common spaces and greenery within our facilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We are also co-locating eldercare and childcare facilities, where possible, to facilitate intergenerational activities, to engage our seniors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We also agree with Dr Lily Neo that it is important for seniors to age in place in the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Hence, we piloted the Care Close to Home programme to support the care and social needs of rental block seniors from Senior Activity Centres.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Care Close to Home is an example on how we enable seniors to age in place by effectively turning these precincts into in-situ "care homes" with assisted living support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: At the same time, we have started building larger day care centres to serve as "Active Ageing Hubs" for seniors that can provide a range of services, from active ageing programmes for healthy and ambulant seniors to day care and rehab services for frail seniors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: One such hub is at Whampoa, which now serves more than 600 seniors across its active ageing and care services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Several Members also asked about respite for caregivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For caregivers who need help for a few hours over the weekend, they can leave their elderly at one of the 10 senior care centres across Singapore, where they will be looked after.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For those who need respite for a longer period, they can have their elderly cared for at nursing homes for several days, up to a month.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In addition, the Eldersitter Programme provides an eldersitter to look after seniors with dementia at their homes when caregiving arrangements are not available.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: On top of this, they can also benefit from the lower foreign domestic worker (FDW) concessionary levy if they hire an FDW.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: If they are from lower- and middle-income families and are caring for an elderly person or a person with moderate disability, they can get an additional FDW grant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We recognise that new cohorts of seniors will have differing aspirations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Our active agers will want to plan ahead for themselves and stay independent for as long as possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We are evolving new models of care and studying new forms of housing that provide seniors with support services as they age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Minister Desmond Lee will touch on this in his speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Dr Lily Neo spoke on the importance of mobility, and I fully agree.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Over 800,000 seniors have benefited from the Passion Silver card since its launch in December 2016, which lets them benefit from cheaper transport and merchant discounts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Our Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) has also partnered Uber to launch UberAssist.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Caregivers and seniors can now use the Uber app to call for a car to take them to their medical appointments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Around 800 drivers have also been trained to date to help assist our seniors, so that they can have a safe journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: More than 96% of our public buses are also wheelchair-accessible, and all will be so by 2020.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: All Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) stations and bus interchanges, and 97% of bus shelters are barrier-free.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Ms Joan Pereira also suggested that we design the signs and notices in public transport to make them easier to read for seniors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Since 2012, all new MRT stations have directional signage with high-contrast colours and larger font sizes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Ministry of Transport (MOT) is in the midst of making similar enhancements to the signs at the older MRT stations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
